title: Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Quantum reservoir computing: using the natural dynamics of a quantum system as a fixed, untrained recurrent network and training only a linear readout, from the classical theory to models, hardware and limits.

children.title: Getting Started
children.summary: The machine-learning ground quantum reservoir computing needs, taught from zero, ending with a two-qubit quantum reservoir worked by hand.

children.title: What Is Reservoir Computing?
children.summary: Reservoir computing is a way of processing signals that unfold in time by letting a fixed, unlearned dynamical system hold a trace of the recent past and training only a simple weighted-sum readout on top of it.

children.title: Time Series and Prediction
children.summary: A time series is a list of measurements in which the order matters, and prediction means producing the next value (or a wanted function of the past) from what has already been seen.

children.title: Neural Networks from Scratch
children.summary: A neural network is a chain of weighted sums, each bent by a nonlinear function, and training means adjusting the weights by following the slope of an error.

children.title: Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout
children.summary: Linear regression fits a weighted sum of measured features to a target by minimising the sum of squared errors, and ridge regression adds a price on large weights so that the fit stays stable.

children.title: Training, Testing and Measuring Error
children.summary: A reservoir readout is only believable when it is scored on data it was not fitted to.

children.title: A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand
children.summary: A complete two-qubit quantum reservoir computer, with every matrix written out: the Hamiltonian, the input written into qubit 1, three time steps computed with numbers, then a few hundred steps in numpy with a ridge readout scored on delay tasks.

children.title: Reservoir Computing Foundations
children.summary: Reservoir computing trains only a linear readout on the states of a fixed, driven dynamical system; everything quantum reservoir computing does is this recipe with a quantum system as the reservoir.

children.title: Echo State Networks
children.summary: An echo state network is a large random recurrent network driven by the input, whose weights are never trained; a linear readout fitted by ridge regression does all the learning.

children.title: The Echo State Property
children.summary: A reservoir has the echo state property when its state, after enough input, is a function of the input history alone and not of where it started.

children.title: Memory and Processing Capacity
children.summary: Memory capacity measures how much of the past input a linear readout can recover from the reservoir state; information processing capacity generalises it to every nonlinear function of the past.

children.title: Physical Reservoirs
children.summary: Because a reservoir is never trained, any physical system with fading memory, nonlinearity and a measurable state can compute: water, light, spins, mechanics.

children.title: Benchmark Tasks and Evaluation
children.summary: Reservoir papers, classical and quantum, report the same handful of tasks: short-term memory, NARMA, parity, Mackey-Glass and similar chaotic series, and channel equalisation.

children.title: Open Quantum Systems Toolkit
children.summary: A quantum reservoir is an open quantum system driven by data: each input step is a quantum channel, its memory is the way that channel forgets, and its output is a noisy estimate of expectation values.

children.title: Density Matrices and Channels
children.summary: A quantum reservoir's state is a density matrix and every input step is a channel acting on it.

children.title: Lindblad Dynamics
children.summary: When a reservoir decays, dephases or is pumped continuously, its evolution in time is a Lindblad (GKSL) master equation.

children.title: Contraction and Fixed Points
children.summary: A quantum reservoir has the echo state property when the channels its inputs select squeeze any two initial states together.

children.title: Measurement
children.summary: A quantum reservoir's features are expectation values, and hardware can only estimate them by measuring, which costs shots and disturbs the state.

children.title: Quantum Reservoir Models
children.summary: A quantum reservoir is a fixed, driven quantum system whose state carries a fading, nonlinear memory of an input stream, with only a linear readout trained.

children.title: The Spin-Network Reservoir
children.summary: The founding QRC model (Fujii and Nakajima 2017) is a few qubits with random all-to-all XX couplings and a Z field, fed by resetting one qubit to an input-dependent state each step and read out through single-qubit Z expectations.

children.title: Input Encoding
children.summary: How a classical number becomes a quantum operation decides which functions of the input a quantum reservoir can represent, which parts of the state the readout can see, and how fast old inputs are forgotten.

children.title: Readout and Multiplexing
children.summary: A quantum reservoir is only as good as the features its readout extracts: which observables are measured, how many times per input, from how many reservoirs, and with how many shots.

children.title: Dynamical Regimes
children.summary: The same spin-network reservoir behaves very differently depending on whether its Hamiltonian is integrable, ergodic or many-body localised, and only some regimes compute well.

children.title: Dissipation as a Resource
children.summary: A closed quantum system never forgets its initial state, so a quantum reservoir needs some non-unitary ingredient (a reset, a measurement or genuine dissipation) to have the echo state property.

children.title: Continuous-Variable Reservoirs
children.summary: A reservoir can be built from bosonic modes (light, microwave resonators, mechanical oscillators) instead of qubits.

children.title: Quantum Extreme Learning Machines
children.summary: A quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) is a quantum reservoir with no memory: each input is encoded into a fresh state, sent through a fixed quantum channel, measured, and fed to a trained linear readout.

children.title: Quantum Data Tasks
children.summary: When the inputs are themselves quantum states, a reservoir can process them without a classical encoding step: the state is fed into the reservoir, measured, and a trained readout estimates its properties.

children.title: Measurement and Hardware
children.summary: On a real device a quantum reservoir's features are not numbers you can read off: each one is an expectation value estimated from repeated destructive measurements, and that single fact sets the cost, the protocol and the accuracy of every physical QRC.

children.title: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise
children.summary: Reading a quantum reservoir disturbs it, and each reading gives only a $\pm 1$ outcome, so a hardware QRC must both protect the memory carried by the state and pay in repetitions for every feature value.

children.title: Online Measurement Protocols
children.summary: Online protocols read the reservoir while it keeps running, trading some disturbance or extra noise for a cost that grows linearly rather than quadratically with the length of the series.

children.title: Gate-Based Devices
children.summary: On a gate-based processor a quantum reservoir is a repeated circuit block (input encoding, a fixed entangling layer, measurement), and the questions are how to compile it, how deep it may be, and whether the device's own noise helps or hurts.

children.title: Analog Platforms
children.summary: Analog quantum devices run a Hamiltonian directly rather than a gate sequence, which suits reservoir computing: the reservoir only needs rich, repeatable dynamics, not programmable precision.

children.title: Resource Accounting
children.summary: Whether a quantum reservoir is practical comes down to arithmetic: how many runs, shots, evolution steps and seconds a task costs on a given protocol and device, set against what the task needs.

children.title: Theory, Limits and Practice
children.summary: What a quantum reservoir can and cannot compute, what it costs as it grows, where a quantum advantage could come from, and a complete reservoir you can run in numpy.

children.title: Expressivity and Universality
children.summary: Which input-output maps a quantum reservoir with a linear readout can approximate: universality for fading-memory filters, the polynomial structure that the input encoding imposes, and hard bounds from feature rank and capacity.

children.title: Concentration and Scalability
children.summary: Why adding qubits does not automatically add usable features: expectation values concentrate exponentially under scrambling and noise, every feature must be estimated from shots, measurement forces restarts, and classical simulation has its own scaling.

children.title: Quantum Advantage
children.summary: What a quantum advantage in reservoir computing would have to mean, the arguments for and against it, which reservoirs are classically simulable, and how to compare against classical models fairly.

children.title: Hands-on Implementation
children.summary: A complete quantum reservoir in numpy: the Hamiltonian, the reset-injection channel, features, a ridge readout, the memory function with and without shot noise, NARMA2 against classical baselines, and an expressivity check.

children.title: Open Problems
children.summary: The questions quantum reservoir computing has not answered yet, from echo state conditions to measurement-efficient learning and a demonstrated advantage, with a self-test across the shelf.
